1.d4 Nc6.name: Bogoljubov–Mikenas Defence
1.d4 Nc6.background: Named after Efim Bogoljubov and Vladas Mikėnas. Hypermodern players such as Aron Nimzowitsch and Bogoljubov tried 1...Nc6, but it has never become very popular.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5.strategy: Gains space by attacking the knight with a pawn that cramps Black's position. It also takes the game out of the usual transpositions. The pawn is advanced early, so White must be ready for Black to strike back at the centre.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4.strategy: Takes more of the centre and queenside space at once. With Black's knight on c6 blocking the c-pawn, Black cannot challenge the pawn pair with ...c5 or ...c6, so White gets a free space edge.

1.d4 Nc6 2.Nf3.strategy: Develops the knight and takes control of e5, the square Black's set-up is built to occupy. White keeps every plan open, while Black's c-pawn is blocked by the knight, which makes many standard queen's pawn set-ups awkward for Black. The most common reply, and a solid one.

1.d4 Nc6 2.e4.strategy: Builds a second central pawn at once. Black's knight is built to challenge exactly that, so White soon has to decide how to meet an attack on the d4 pawn; the result is a sharper game in which White's space can turn into a target.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5.strategy: Strikes at once: the d4-pawn is attacked by the pawn and the knight and defended only by the queen. White must settle the tension, and Black gets a say in the centre in exchange for the time the knight took.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 d5.strategy: Challenges the centre with a pawn and uses the knight on c6 to pressure d4, instead of building the usual solid chain with ...c6. The cost is that the c-pawn is blocked, so the d5 pawn has less support and can come under pressure. A respectable, somewhat sharper way to meet the move.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops a piece and prepares a quick strike with the e-pawn, backed by the knight on c6. Black fights for the centre with pieces and a pawn break instead of a solid chain: sound but offbeat, and the game turns tactical quickly. White can also gain space by pushing the d-pawn.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.d5.strategy: Saves the d4-pawn by driving the knight away and gains space with tempo. White gets a spacious, closed centre; Black must find a good square for the knight and then undermine the pawn chain.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5.strategy: Gives up the central tension and the space gained. After the knight recaptures, it attacks the c4-pawn, which nothing defends, so White must spend time or offer the pawn while Black's knight is already active.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops and adds a defender to d4, but lets Black decide what comes next. Black can liquidate the centre for an equal, simplified game, or push the e-pawn forward to gain space with tempo on the knight, so White has not kept the initiative.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.d5 Nce7.name: Bogoljubov–Mikenas Defence: Lithuanian Variation
1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.d5 Nce7.strategy: Steps back to a flexible square, from which the knight eyes the d5-pawn and can go to g6. Black concedes space for a compact position with a strong e5 pawn, and prepares to attack White's centre with a pawn break in a closed game.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.d5 Nd4.name: Bogoljubov–Mikenas Defence: Cannstatter Variation
1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.d5 Nd4.strategy: Centralises the knight on a square protected by the e5-pawn. But White can drive it away with e3 and gain a tempo, and the knight has little future there, so Black risks falling behind in development against White's space edge.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.d5 Nb8.strategy: Takes the knight back to its starting square, which costs time but keeps it from being harassed and leaves the e5 pawn intact. White has the space; Black has a compact position without weaknesses and the later chance to attack the pawn chain.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5.strategy: Recaptures with a centralised knight that attacks the loose c4-pawn. White must give a pawn or spend a tempo to protect it, so Black quickly gets active play for free.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Bb4+.strategy: Develops with check and keeps the knight's attack on e5. White must spend a move meeting the check, so Black regains the pawn with a developed bishop and an active position; if White blocks with the knight, that knight is pinned.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Nge7.strategy: Develops the second knight and keeps the attack on e5 from c6. White can simply hold the extra pawn with Nf3, which also develops, so Black has given up the quick recapture and is a pawn down. Black gets active piece play, but has to earn it.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops instead of defending the pawn, offering c4 as a gambit for quick development and open lines. It is a real gambit, not a free one: Black can take the pawn and keep it if White has no punishing follow-up.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.e4.strategy: Answers the threat to c4 and builds the centre in one move: the bishop now guards the pawn, so ...Nxc4 would simply lose a piece. White gets two central pawns and the space, and Black has to undermine that centre with piece play.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.e3.strategy: Also guards c4, the f1-bishop now seeing it, and keeps the position solid. The cost is a passive bishop on c1, shut in behind the pawn, and a slower build-up, so Black develops freely and starts with a check on b4.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.Nc3 Nxc4.name: Bogoljubov–Mikenas Defence: Pozarek Gambit
1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.Nc3 Nxc4.strategy: Accepts the gambit and keeps the pawn: after 5.Qd4 the knight drops back to b6, since the bishop covers g7. The knight has left the centre and Black must develop accurately, but a clean extra pawn is worth the effort.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.Nc3 Bb4.strategy: Develops with a pin: the knight on c3 cannot move without exposing the king on the open diagonal, while the c4 pawn is still attacked. Black builds pressure before grabbing the pawn; the risk is a queen move to d4 that hits the knight on e5 and demands accurate play.

1.d4 Nc6 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Nxe5 4.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the second knight and watches e4 and d5, but leaves the c4 pawn alone, so White has time to deal with it. Black gives up the chance to win a pawn for steady development: playable, but it does not test White's gambit.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8.name: Montevideo Defence
1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8.strategy: Goes back to the start square, which looks like a lost tempo but costs little: White has only gained space, and the advanced pawn on d5 needs support and can become a target. Black rebuilds solidly rather than risk the knight on an exposed square.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Ne5.strategy: Moves the knight to the best central square, away from the pawn, where it eyes c4, d3 and f3. White can chase it and gain space with tempo, but the advancing pawns leave targets, which is the idea of the whole set-up: Black lets White overextend, then strikes at the centre.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb4.strategy: Sends the knight to the edge, where it threatens nothing real: a3 chases it away with tempo, and the retreat squares are poor. Black loses more time than with a plain retreat while White keeps the space gained by the pawn on d5.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nd4.strategy: Hangs the knight: the queen on d1 sees d4 along the open d-file and nothing defends the knight, so White simply takes it with 3.Qxd4.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8 3.e4.strategy: Makes the most of the lost time: Black's knight has gone to c6 and back, so White claims a broad pawn centre with the d5 pawn already taking c6 and e6 from Black's pieces. Black has to attack the centre rather than occupy it.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8 3.c4.strategy: Backs up the d5 pawn with the c-pawn and takes space on the queenside, so the advanced pawn is hard to challenge. It is a slower way to use the extra tempo than the e-pawn thrust, but it builds a lasting space advantage and leaves White the choice of how to complete the centre.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8 3.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece and watches the e5 square, so Black cannot comfortably play ...e5. It is sound but quiet: White leaves the extra tempo largely unused and does not take the broad centre, which gives Black time to organise a challenge to the d5 pawn.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8 3.e4 Nf6.strategy: Challenges the e4 pawn and develops, the natural way to fight the centre, but the pawn can simply advance with gain of time. Black has spent most of the opening moving the same knight around, and White's space grows.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8 3.e4 d6.strategy: Meets the broad centre with a solid pawn: it guards c5 and e5 and opens the c8-bishop's diagonal. Black gives White the space but builds a compact set-up with few targets, and plans to undermine the centre later. White keeps the initiative, but nothing here is forced.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8 3.e4 e6.strategy: Hits the d5 pawn at once and opens a diagonal for the king's bishop. The price is that White can take on e6: if Black recaptures with the d-pawn, a queen trade leaves Black's king uncastled, and recapturing with the f-pawn loosens Black's kingside.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8 3.e4 Nf6 4.e5.strategy: Gains space and a tempo in one move: the pawn attacks the knight, and every square it can reach is one more move that Black spends on the knight instead of on development. The advanced pawns will need support later, but they cramp Black's position.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8 3.e4 Nf6 4.Nc3.strategy: Defends the e4 pawn with a developing move, so Black's knight cannot simply take it. White keeps the e-pawn's advance in reserve and keeps a healthy lead in space and development; the slower move gives Black a moment to challenge the d5 pawn.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8 3.e4 Nf6 4.Bd3.strategy: Defends the e4 pawn with a developing move and prepares to castle. It is sound but modest: the bishop blocks the queen's line down the d-file and the b1-knight stays at home, so White uses the space less actively than with the pawn thrust or the knight move.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8 3.e4 Nf6 4.e5 Ng8.name: Zaire Defence
1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8 3.e4 Nf6 4.e5 Ng8.strategy: Retreats to the starting square: after four knight moves Black has made no progress, while White holds a broad pawn centre at no cost. Nothing hangs, but Black must start developing from scratch behind it.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8 3.e4 Nf6 4.e5 Ne4.strategy: The only square where the knight stays in play: g4 and h5 lose it to the queen, and d5 is guarded by the queen down the d-file. White can harass it with f3 or Qd3, but each such move costs time. Black keeps a piece in the game instead of returning to the start.

1.d4 Nc6 2.d5 Nb8 3.e4 Nf6 4.e5 Nxd5.strategy: Grabs a pawn and loses a piece: the d5 pawn is guarded by the queen down the open d-file, and Qxd5 wins the knight for a pawn with no compensation.
